title: How Go fails in production
summary: Reading the crash, telling panic from fatal, and finding the leak.

concepts.title: Reading a panic
concepts.brief:
The first word tells you what kind of failure it is, and whether anything could have caught it:

- **`panic:`** — recoverable in principle, deferred functions ran during the unwind.
- **`fatal error:`** — not recoverable, no defers ran. The runtime judged the process unsalvageable.

Then: `goroutine 42 [running]:` names the goroutine and its state, and the frames follow **innermost first**. Skip the ones under `/usr/local/go/src/` — the deepest frame in *your* code is where to look.

A `[signal SIGSEGV ... addr=0x0]` line under a panic means a nil pointer was dereferenced. `addr=0x0` is the giveaway.

examples.label: A nil pointer dereference, annotated
examples.code:
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x0 pc=0x6f2a1c]

goroutine 42 [running]:
main.(*Store).Lookup(0x0, {0xc000184120, 0x5})
        /app/store.go:31 +0x1c
main.handle({0x8a1f60, 0xc0001a4000}, 0xc0001b8100)
        /app/main.go:58 +0x8d
examples.note: `addr=0x0` says nil. `main.(*Store).Lookup(0x0, ...)` shows the receiver *is* 0x0 — a nil `*Store`, so the bug is whoever constructed it, at main.go:58.

examples.label: The states a goroutine can be parked in
examples.code:
[running]        actually executing
[runnable]       waiting for a processor
[chan send]      blocked sending - nobody receiving
[chan receive]   blocked receiving - nobody sending
[select]         blocked in a select, no case ready
[semacquire]     waiting on a mutex or WaitGroup
[IO wait]        in a network read or write
[sleep]          in time.Sleep
examples.note: In a goroutine profile, the state plus the line is usually the whole diagnosis: thousands at `[chan send]` on one line means the receivers are gone.

items.prompt: A crash log starts `fatal error: concurrent map writes`. What does the first word tell you?
choices: No recover could have caught it, and no deferred functions ran
The same as panic, with more severe wording
The error came from cgo rather than Go code
The process was killed by the OS, not the runtime
items.explain: `fatal error:` bypasses the panic machinery entirely — no unwinding, no defers, no recover. The runtime uses it when continuing would corrupt state. So if someone says "we recovered it and it still died", the first word explains why. Fix the map with a mutex; there is no catching this one.

items.prompt: `[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x0 pc=0x6f2a1c]`. What does `addr=0x0` tell you?
choices: A nil pointer was dereferenced — address zero
The stack overflowed
Memory was corrupted by cgo
The binary was built for the wrong architecture
items.explain: Address zero is nil. In Go a SIGSEGV almost always means a nil pointer rather than genuine memory corruption, because the language has no pointer arithmetic. Look at the innermost frame of your own code: if the receiver is printed as `0x0`, the method was called on a nil value and the real bug is at the construction site.

items.prompt: Put the steps of reading an unfamiliar panic in order.
steps: Read the first word: panic or fatal error
Read the message itself to classify it - nil map, index, nil pointer
Find the deepest frame that is in your own code, not the standard library
Look at that line's inputs - which one could have been nil or out of range
items.explain: Frames are printed innermost first, so your code is usually a few lines down, under the runtime's own frames. The standard library is rarely the bug: it is where your bad value finally got used. Working from the deepest *application* frame is faster than reading top to bottom.

items.prompt: Match each runtime message to its cause.
pairs: assignment to entry in nil map
A map was declared but never made
index out of range [5] with length 3
A slice index past the end
interface conversion: ... is string, not int
items.explain: The first three are panics and name the exact value involved, which usually makes the fix obvious. The fourth is a fatal error and only fires when *nothing* is runnable — so a server with a live listener never gets this message no matter how much is stuck.

concepts.title: Memory, the GC and OOMKilled
concepts.brief:
Go's garbage collector targets a **heap size**, not a memory ceiling. By default `GOGC=100` means it lets the heap grow to roughly twice the live set before collecting — so a service with 300MB live will happily use 600MB, and a container limit of 512Mi kills it.

**`GOMEMLIMIT`** (Go 1.19+) is the fix: a soft limit that makes the GC work harder as you approach it, instead of being killed. Set it a little below the container limit — 90% is a common choice — so there is headroom for stacks and off-heap allocations.

An OOMKill with no Go error in the log is the normal shape: the kernel kills the process, so there is nothing for Go to print.

examples.label: Giving the GC the container's budget
examples.code:
env:
  - name: GOMEMLIMIT
    value: "920MiB"      # ~90% of the limit below
  - name: GOMAXPROCS
    value: "2"
resources:
  limits:
    memory: 1Gi
    cpu: "2"
examples.note: Go 1.25 makes GOMAXPROCS cgroup-aware, so setting it by hand matters less on newer runtimes — GOMEMLIMIT still has to be set deliberately.

examples.label: Watching the collector work
examples.code:
$ GODEBUG=gctrace=1 ./app
gc 1 @0.021s 0%: ... 4->4->1 MB, 5 MB goal, 0 MB stacks, 0 MB globals, 8 P
examples.note: `4->4->1 MB` is heap size at GC start, at GC end, and live afterwards; `5 MB goal` is the next trigger. Rising live size across cycles is a real leak rather than GC lag.

items.prompt: A pod with a 512Mi limit is OOMKilled. Live heap is around 300MB and there is no Go error in the log. Why?
choices: GOGC=100 lets the heap reach ~2x live before collecting, overshooting the limit
A goroutine leak; live heap would otherwise be stable
The GC is disabled by default in container builds
The log is missing because the panic went to stdout rather than stderr
items.explain: The GC targets a heap *ratio*, and knows nothing about the cgroup limit unless you tell it. 300MB live with GOGC=100 aims for about 600MB, which exceeds 512Mi, and the kernel kills the process before Go can react — hence no error at all. Set `GOMEMLIMIT` to roughly 90% of the limit.

items.prompt: What does GOMEMLIMIT do when the limit is approached?
choices: The GC runs more aggressively to stay under it — it is a soft limit
Allocations start returning errors
The program panics with out of memory
It is a hard cap enforced by the runtime allocator
items.explain: Soft: Go collects harder rather than failing, trading CPU for memory. If the live set genuinely exceeds it you get GC thrashing — high CPU and little progress — which is a clearer signal than a silent kill, and survivable long enough to notice. It does not replace fixing the leak.

items.prompt: Why does an OOMKilled Go container usually leave no stack trace?
choices: The kernel kills the process with SIGKILL — Go gets no chance to print
Go catches SIGKILL and writes a trace, but the container is gone before it flushes
Out-of-memory is a fatal error, and those print nothing
The trace is written but truncated by the container runtime
items.explain: SIGKILL cannot be handled, so the process is simply gone. Reach for the pod's previous-state exit code — 137 is SIGKILL — and for the kernel's OOM message, rather than looking for an application log that will never exist. Go's own `fatal error: out of memory` only appears when the Go allocator fails first.

items.prompt: Memory is climbing steadily. Which of these distinguish a leak from normal GC behavior?
choices: The live heap after each GC rises across cycles rather than returning to a baseline
The goroutine count rises monotonically
The heap profile shows one allocation site growing without bound
RSS is higher than the live heap
items.explain: The first three are real signals. RSS above live heap is normal and expected — Go keeps freed memory mapped for reuse and returns it to the OS lazily, so comparing RSS to heap size tells you very little on its own.

concepts.title: pprof, and what to collect
concepts.brief:
`import _ "net/http/pprof"` registers handlers under `/debug/pprof/` on the default mux. Expose it on a port that is not public.

- **`/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=1`** — counts and stacks, grouped. The first thing to pull for a hang or a climbing-memory problem.
- **`/debug/pprof/heap`** — what is allocated *now*, by allocation site.
- **`/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30`** — a CPU profile over a window.

`go tool pprof` reads any of them. The single most useful command once it is open is `top`, then `list <function>` to see the cost line by line.

examples.label: Pulling and reading a profile
examples.code:
# count goroutines, grouped by stack
$ curl -s localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=1 | head

# interactive, against a live process
$ go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap
(pprof) top
(pprof) list myFunc
examples.note: Profiles are small and cheap to collect. The goroutine one is effectively free; a CPU profile costs a few percent for its window.

items.prompt: Match the symptom to the profile you should pull first.
pairs: Requests hang but the process is alive
goroutine — see what they block on
items.explain: The goroutine profile answers two very different questions, which is why it is usually the first thing to grab: it shows both leaks and hangs, and it is cheap enough to collect on a struggling process.

items.prompt: You add `import _ "net/http/pprof"` but never reference the package. Why does it still work?
choices: Its init() registers the handlers on http.DefaultServeMux
The compiler links it because the import is blank
The runtime scans for debug packages at startup
It does not — you must call pprof.Register()
items.explain: Side-effect import. The catch is that it registers on `http.DefaultServeMux`, so if your service uses a custom mux you will not see the routes — and if it serves the default mux publicly, you have just exposed profiling to the internet. Run it on a separate internal listener.

items.prompt: A Go service is using more memory every hour. Put the triage in order.
steps: Check whether the goroutine count is rising monotonically
If it is, pull the goroutine profile and group the stacks
If it is not, pull the heap profile and find the growing allocation site
Set GOMEMLIMIT as a stopgap so the pod degrades instead of being killed
items.explain: Goroutines first, because a goroutine leak explains a memory leak and the check costs one number. Only if goroutines are flat is it worth reading the heap profile. `GOMEMLIMIT` is a mitigation, not a fix — it buys time to find the cause without a crash loop.

items.prompt: Should you run the race detector in production to catch an intermittent data race?
choices: No — it costs several times the CPU and memory; run it in tests and staging
Yes, it is designed for production use
Yes, but only with GOMAXPROCS=1
No, because it only works on test binaries
items.explain: `-race` instruments every memory access: expect a large slowdown and much higher memory. It works on any binary, not just tests, so a race-enabled build in staging under realistic load is a reasonable middle ground. It only reports races it actually observes, so it needs the code path to execute.
